title: Vectors | Chapter 1, Essence of linear algebra
summary: The first chapter of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, introducing vectors with animated geometric visuals. It begins a series that builds intuition for linear algebra from the basics.
why_hn: HN's go-to recommendation for learning linear algebra intuition, repeatedly credited with making concepts click and complementing textbooks.

title: How to Speak
summary: Patrick Winston's long-running MIT lecture on public speaking teaches heuristic rules for talks. It covers how to start, use time and place, boards, props and slides, and how to inform, persuade and finish.
why_hn: HN treats it as the canonical, near-universally recommended lecture on giving talks and presentations.

title: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
summary: Andrej Karpathy's first Neural Networks: Zero to Hero lecture, which builds micrograd, a tiny autograd engine, from scratch in Python. It explains backpropagation and neural network training step by step, assuming only basic Python and some high-school calculus.
why_hn: HN treats it as the best starting point for really understanding backprop and neural nets, because Karpathy explains the why with intuition and builds everything in code.

title: 8 Bit & '8 Bitish' Graphics-Outside the Box
summary: Mark Ferrari, the LucasArts background artist, explains in a GDC 2016 talk how he draws 8-bit graphics. He covers color cycling and palette shifting to create complex animated scenery without frame animation.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as a master class in limited-palette pixel art and palette cycling, from an artist behind Loom and Monkey Island.

title: In Search Of A Flat Earth
summary: Dan Olson's 76-minute essay on flat earth belief, built around a hike to a lake to test earth's curvature. It examines the community, how YouTube promoted it, and how it connects to wider conspiracy thinking and QAnon.
why_hn: HN treats it as the definitive, compassionate documentary on why people fall into conspiracy theories.

title: 1. Introduction to Human Behavioral Biology
summary: The opening lecture of Robert Sapolsky's Stanford course on Human Behavioral Biology, explaining the course premise and how to avoid categorical thinking. It starts a roughly 25-lecture series on how biology, genes, hormones and environment shape behavior.
why_hn: One of the most consistently recommended lecture series on HN, praised as fascinating, funny and eye-opening about human behavior across many scales.

title: How The Economic Machine Works by Ray Dalio
summary: Ray Dalio's 30-minute animated video explains how the economy works through credit, debt, interest rates, and short- and long-term cycles. It is based on his template for understanding the economy.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the best layperson overview of debt, credit and economic cycles.

title: But what is the Fourier Transform?  A visual introduction.
summary: 3Blue1Brown's animated visual introduction to the Fourier Transform, showing how a signal breaks into frequency components.
why_hn: HN's default recommendation for understanding the Fourier transform intuitively; many say it was the explanation that made it click.

title: Essential Ideas for Parents
summary: Dr. Russell Barkley's roughly three-hour lecture on ADHD for parents of affected children. It explains what ADHD is and how the ADHD brain differs.
why_hn: Repeatedly called the best way to understand ADHD, and recommended to anyone before commenting on it.

title: Try to Rule Fairly and You'll Be Overthrown
summary: CGP Grey's animated adaptation of The Dictator's Handbook, explaining how rulers stay in power by keeping a small group of key supporters happy rather than ruling fairly. It lays out selectorate theory and how resources shape regimes.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard short summary of how power and political incentives work, applied to governments, companies and workplaces.

title: But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1
summary: 3Blue1Brown's first chapter on deep learning explains what neurons and layers are and the math underlying a basic neural network, using handwritten digit recognition with visual animations.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard first stop for learning neural networks, praised for making the math intuitive.

title: A Better Default Colormap for Matplotlib | SciPy 2015 | Nathaniel Smith and Stéfan van der Walt
summary: SciPy 2015 talk by Nathaniel Smith and Stefan van der Walt on choosing a new default colormap for Matplotlib. It covers why Jet misleads, how perceptual color spaces work, and how viridis was designed.
why_hn: HN's go-to recommendation for colormap and color-perception questions; commenters call it funny, brief, clear and a favorite talk.

title: George Lakoff: Moral Politics
summary: Cognitive scientist George Lakoff lectures on how political debates are framed through language and metaphors tied to values, and on the moral worldviews behind progressive and conservative politics. It was given in 2005 at UC San Diego.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly say it changed how they hear political speech and recommend it for understanding why opponents are not simply stupid.

title: The Century of the Self (Full Adam Curtis Documentary)
summary: Adam Curtis' multi-part documentary on how Freud's ideas and Edward Bernays' public relations shaped consumer culture and political control. It argues that business and government learned to manufacture desires.
why_hn: HN recommends it often and strongly as an eye-opening account of marketing psychology and the engineering of consumer society.

title: Dominion (2018) - full documentary [Official]
summary: Dominion is a two-hour documentary using drones and hidden cameras to expose conditions in animal agriculture, including food, clothing, entertainment and research. It questions humanity's dominion over animals.
why_hn: HN commenters push it, often forcefully, as the video to watch to see what factory farming really involves, and some say it changed their diet.

title: SM64 - Watch for Rolling Rocks - 0.5x A Presses (Commentated) [OUTDATED]
summary: Pannenkoek2012's commentated tool-assisted Super Mario 64 run collecting the Watch for Rolling Rocks star with half an A press, using parallel universes and QPU movement. The video is marked outdated in favor of a newer version.
why_hn: Held up as a legendary deep dive into game internals, explained lucidly and with humor, and a gateway to the channel.

title: MIT's Pathway to Fusion Energy (IAP 2017) - Zach Hartwig
channel: MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center
summary: Zach Hartwig of MIT introduces the key concepts of magnetic fusion energy and the state of fusion research. He then presents MIT's proposed pathway of using high-field superconducting magnets to build smaller, cheaper tokamaks on a climate-relevant timescale.
why_hn: Recommended again and again as the best accessible overview of fusion physics, useful for judging fusion announcements and understanding why high-temperature superconducting magnets matter.

title: Stanford's Sapolsky On Depression in U.S. (Full Lecture)
summary: Stanford professor Robert Sapolsky lectures on depression as a real biological disease. He covers its biological and psychological causes, how it differs from ordinary sadness, and ideas such as learned helplessness. He ties these together into one account.
why_hn: HN returns to it repeatedly as the best single introduction to understanding clinical depression.

title: Justice: What's The Right Thing To Do? Episode 01 "THE MORAL SIDE OF MURDER"
summary: The first episode of Michael Sandel's Harvard course on moral reasoning, opening with the trolley problem and the choice between killing one to save five. Sandel draws out student arguments and introduces utilitarian and other approaches to justice.
why_hn: One of the most frequently recommended online lecture series on HN, praised for giving people vocabulary to examine ethical positions and for Sandel's skilled teaching.

title: Video explains the world's most important 6-sec drum loop
summary: Nate Harrison's 2004 video history of the Amen Break, a six-second drum sample from a 1969 b-side that became the basis of hip-hop sampling, jungle and drum and bass. It is also a meditation on cultural ownership and creativity.
why_hn: A perennial HN recommendation, brought up whenever sampling, copyright or music history comes up, often described as a must-watch.

title: Reverse emulating the NES to give it SUPER POWERS!
summary: Tom Murphy (suckerpinch) shows 'reverse emulation', using a Raspberry Pi in an NES cartridge to give an unmodified NES new abilities such as playing SNES games. The video starts in a strange way and gets stranger.
why_hn: Praised as a brilliant, deadpan and inventive hardware hack, and a good starting point for Tom7's videos.

title: Sugar: THE BITTER TRUTH
summary: Robert Lustig of UCSF lectures on the biochemistry of sugar, arguing that fructose and lack of fiber drive the obesity epidemic via insulin. It is the widely viewed 90-minute talk that popularized the anti-sugar case.
why_hn: The most-linked YouTube video on HN, recommended as an in-depth explanation of fructose metabolism.

title: Steve Jobs Stanford Commencement Speech 2005
summary: Steve Jobs's 2005 Stanford commencement address, built around three stories: connecting the dots, love and loss including being fired from Apple, and death. It is a 15-minute talk on finding work you love.
why_hn: HN returns to it for years as an inspirational talk to send to graduates, founders and anyone at a career crossroads.

title: What Bodies Think About: Bioelectric Computation Outside the Nervous System - NeurIPS 2018
summary: Michael Levin's NeurIPS 2018 talk on bioelectric computation outside the nervous system, showing how cell electrical networks shape development and regeneration. It covers morphological information processing in living tissue.
why_hn: HN regularly calls it mind-blowing and recommends it as an introduction to Levin's work on bioelectricity and regeneration.

title: What Happened to Horses Is Happening to Us
summary: CGP Grey's video "Humans Need Not Apply" argues that automation will make a large part of the workforce economically obsolete, much as engines did for horses. It surveys robots and software replacing both physical and mental labor.
why_hn: HN has recommended it for a decade as the standard explainer on automation and unemployment, though skeptics later cite it as an example of overconfident predictions.

title: James Burke Connections, Ep. 1 "The Trigger Effect"
summary: The first episode of James Burke's 1978 BBC series Connections traces modern dependence on complex technological networks, starting with the 1965 New York blackout, and moves through ancient agriculture to Kuwait's oil-driven leap.
why_hn: Heavily recommended as a masterpiece of popular science and the classic illustration of how fragile interdependent systems are, trotted out in every blackout or supply chain thread.

title: Project Code Rush - The Beginnings of Netscape / Mozilla Documentary
summary: Code Rush is a one-hour documentary following Netscape engineers in Silicon Valley through the company's last year as an independent firm. It covers the Mozilla open-source announcement, the frantic push to ready the source for release by March 31, 1998, and the toll on engineers' lives before the AOL acquisition.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an intimate, embedded look at late-90s web history and the spirit of building something important under pressure.

title: DON'T PANIC — Hans Rosling showing the facts about population
summary: Hans Rosling uses data and animated statistics to show how world population is changing, why birth rates fall as child survival and wealth rise, and why population is expected to peak around 11 billion. It also tackles common misconceptions about Africa and family planning.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it to counter overpopulation alarm with data on falling birth rates.

title: Velocity NY 2013:   Richard Cook, "Resilience In Complex Adaptive Systems"
summary: Richard Cook's short Velocity 2013 talk on resilience in complex adaptive systems, arguing systems operate near the edge of failure and that the surprise is how rarely they fail. He presents a model of how pressures push systems toward failure boundaries.
why_hn: HN people cite it constantly as the clearest explanation of normalization of deviance and how complex systems drift toward failure.

title: AlphaGo - The Movie | Full award-winning documentary
summary: Feature-length documentary following DeepMind's AlphaGo program as it prepares for and plays the 2016 match against Go champion Lee Sedol. It covers the team, the games, and the emotional reaction of the Go world to an AI beating a top human.
why_hn: HN commenters call it a moving, well-made human story about AI and Go that works for non-technical viewers and does not date.

title: We Were Taught to Call Death a Blessing
summary: CGP Grey narrates an animated adaptation of Nick Bostrom's Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant. The story uses a dragon that demands a daily toll of lives as a metaphor for aging and society's acceptance of death.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it in longevity and aging threads as a concise, fun case for fighting aging.

title: Don't Talk to the Police
summary: Regent Law professor James Duane gives startling reasons why people, even innocent ones, should always exercise their Fifth Amendment rights rather than talk to police. It is based on his article and book on the subject.
why_hn: HN treats it as the canonical video to link whenever talking to police or interrogations come up.

title: Randy Pausch's Last Lecture: Achieving Your Childhood Dreams
summary: Randy Pausch's 2007 last lecture at Carnegie Mellon, given as he was dying of pancreatic cancer. He reflects on achieving childhood dreams, overcoming obstacles and helping others reach theirs.
why_hn: Perennially recommended as an inspirational talk for people facing setbacks or choosing a direction, and a source of oft-quoted lines like the brick wall.

title: The great porn experiment | Gary Wilson | TEDxGlasgow
summary: Gary Wilson's TEDxGlasgow talk argues that internet pornography hyperstimulates the brain's reward system and can cause symptoms that reverse when people stop. TED notes that several claims are not supported by respected academic studies.
why_hn: HN commenters frequently recommend it as an eye-opening case against heavy porn use, though it is contested science.

title: Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order by Ray Dalio
summary: An animated 44-minute summary of Ray Dalio's book Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order. It lays out the Big Cycle of rising and declining nations, covering debt cycles, internal conflict, and shifts in global power over the past 500 years.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a clear framework for placing the current US and world situation within historical debt and empire cycles.

title: YouTube's copyright system isn't broken. The world's is.
summary: Tom Scott's long explainer on YouTube's copyright system, Content ID and the DMCA. He argues the platform's system is a workaround for a broader copyright system that does not fit the modern world.
why_hn: The default link in copyright and takedown threads, recommended as an excellent, comprehensive explanation of why automated enforcement and the law work as they do.

title: Ed Catmull, Pixar: Keep Your Crises Small
summary: Ed Catmull of Pixar speaks at Stanford's 2007 Entrepreneurship Conference on running a creative company. He argues for surfacing small problems early and building good teams, with stories like the Toy Story 2 crunch.
why_hn: Repeatedly called one of the most useful talks on building organizations and managing creative teams.

title: Alain de Botton: Status Anxiety
summary: Alain de Botton's 2004 documentary based on his book Status Anxiety, running over two hours. It asks why people in rich societies are still unhappy, and examines how worries about success, snobbery and meritocracy drive that anxiety.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an illuminating, eye-opening long-form take on status, luck and how we judge the successful and unsuccessful.

title: The Most IMPORTANT Video You'll Ever See (part 1 of 8)
summary: Part 1 of a lecture by physicist Albert Bartlett on the exponential function and its consequences for population growth, resource use and energy. It argues that steady growth rates quickly lead to enormous quantities.
why_hn: A perennial HN recommendation for building intuition about exponential growth, cited whenever endless growth, energy or population come up.

title: The Ultimate Game Boy Talk (33c3)
summary: Michael Steil's 33c3 talk explains essentially everything about the Game Boy: CPU, video hardware, peripherals, and the tricks used by games and demos. It revives the era of counting clock cycles around hardware limits.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard starting point for Game Boy emulator writers and homebrew developers, with several calling it one of their favorite talks.

title: Stroads are Ugly, Expensive, and Dangerous (and they're everywhere) [ST05]
summary: Not Just Bikes introduces the "stroad", a street-road hybrid common in the US and Canada that fails at both jobs. He contrasts it with Dutch design, where each road has a single purpose, and covers cost, danger and ugliness.
why_hn: HN links it constantly as the standard introduction to stroads and Strong Towns-style arguments about car-centric design.

title: Controlling Your Dopamine For Motivation, Focus & Satisfaction
summary: Andrew Huberman's long Huberman Lab episode is a masterclass on dopamine. It covers the neural circuits, peaks and baselines, dopamine depletion, and 14 tools for motivation, focus and avoiding addiction.
why_hn: HN recommends it repeatedly to people struggling with motivation, distraction or phone and internet addiction, as a science-based guide to dopamine.

title: ADHD: Essential Ideas for Parents - Dr. Russell Barkely
summary: Dr. Russell Barkley gives a nearly three-hour lecture of essential ideas about ADHD for parents, covering what ADHD is, its effects on executive function, motivation and emotion, and how it affects children.
why_hn: HN readers recommend it as the best primer for understanding ADHD at a neurological level, often suggesting that even the first 10 to 20 minutes are enlightening.

title: USENIX Security '18-Q: Why Do Keynote Speakers Keep Suggesting That Improving Security Is Possible?
summary: James Mickens's humorous USENIX Security keynote argues that improving security and trusting opaque technology like machine learning is far harder than the industry admits.
why_hn: HN considers it a classic, hilarious and sobering talk on ML inscrutability and tech hubris, often rewatched.

title: Music and Life - Alan Watts
summary: A two-minute animation of an Alan Watts talk arguing that life is like music: it is meant to be danced to in the moment, not rushed toward a final goal. It is a short, accessible take on living in the present.
why_hn: HN commenters post it in threads about purpose, ambition, burnout and career anxiety as a reframing that life is a dance, not a march toward eventual happiness.

title: Harder Drive: Hard drives we didn't want or need
summary: Tom7 (suckerpinch) builds and evaluates a series of absurd hard drives, including storage made from ping packets across the internet. The video accompanies his paper and mixes deep technical hacking with comedic storytelling.
why_hn: HN treats it as a favorite example of silly but educational computer science, recommended often when threads touch odd storage hacks.

title: The Solar Gravitational Lens will Map Exoplanets. Seriously.
summary: Explains the proposed NASA JPL plan to use the Sun as a gravitational lens, sending solar sail craft to its focal region to image an exoplanet's surface. It covers the distances involved, how imaging with the Sun would work and the mission design.
why_hn: HN strongly recommends it as the clearest, best-illustrated explanation of the solar gravitational lens idea, and links it whenever exoplanet imaging comes up.

title: Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek - The Original Economics Rap Battle!
summary: A rap battle in which John Maynard Keynes and F. A. Hayek debate the causes of boom and bust, stimulus, and bailouts. It was produced by Econstories to teach the two schools of thought.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a funny, accurate and easy primer on Keynesian versus Austrian views of the business cycle.

title: Hammock Driven Development - Rich Hickey
summary: Rich Hickey's philosophical talk from the first Clojure Conj in 2010. He argues that good design comes from deliberate, away-from-keyboard thinking, and describes how to feed the background mind so it solves problems.
why_hn: HN returns to it constantly as permission and method for thinking deeply before coding, and as an antidote to always-working anxiety.

title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
summary: Andrej Karpathy's three-hour-plus general-audience deep dive into how ChatGPT-style LLMs are built, covering the full training stack from pretraining to post-training. It also gives mental models for their quirks, like hallucination, and how to use them well.
why_hn: HN's most frequent recommendation for a clear, approachable foundation in how LLMs work without heavy math.

title: The Century of the Self - Part 1: "Happiness Machines"
summary: The first part of Adam Curtis' documentary series on Sigmund Freud and his nephew Edward Bernays, who invented public relations. It shows how Bernays used Freud's ideas to link mass-produced goods to unconscious desires and create modern consumer persuasion.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it constantly in threads about advertising, propaganda and manipulation as the origin story of the consumer society.

title: Brian Beckman: Don't fear the Monad
summary: Microsoft's Brian Beckman gives an hour-long, whiteboard-style walk through monads, building from function composition and monoids using school-level math. It is aimed at practicing programmers rather than category theorists.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the clearest and most correct beginner explanation of monads, with several commenters saying it finally made them click.

title: Joe Rogan Experience #1035 - Paul Stamets
summary: A two-hour Joe Rogan Experience conversation with mycologist Paul Stamets about fungi, mycelium, bioremediation and medicinal mushrooms. It touches on Lion's Mane, psilocybin and the many uses of fungi.
why_hn: Commenters offer it as a fascinating, accessible introduction to the world of fungi whenever mushrooms or mycelium come up.

title: RSA ANIMATE: Drive: The surprising truth about what motivates us
summary: An RSA Animate whiteboard adaptation of Dan Pink's talk on what motivates people at work. It argues that beyond simple tasks, autonomy, mastery and purpose drive performance more than money.
why_hn: HN uses it in discussions of pay, management, and motivation as the standard short explanation of autonomy, mastery and purpose.

title: Why Being Delusional is a Superpower
summary: Veritasium examines the role of luck in success, with simulations and examples showing how small advantages and chance can compound. It argues that top outcomes are disproportionately luck-driven while still crediting effort.
why_hn: Linked in threads about meritocracy, careers and startups as a reminder that luck shapes who ends up on top.

title: Personal Growth Series: Dr. William Dement on Healthy Sleep and Optimal Perfo...
summary: A Google Tech Talk by sleep researcher Dr. William Dement on healthy sleep and performance. He argues sleep debt must be repaid and describes the three characteristics of healthy sleep.
why_hn: HN has recommended it for years as the most useful and entertaining talk on sleep, often to people struggling with tiredness or productivity.

title: Marty Lobdell - Study Less Study Smart
summary: Psychology professor Marty Lobdell gives a one-hour lecture on how to study effectively, covering short focused sessions with breaks, study environment, note-taking and memory techniques. It was aimed at students who cram without improving.
why_hn: HN recommends it for productivity, focus and working-from-home threads, since its advice on breaks and mental modes applies beyond studying.

title: You Need a Theme, Not a Goal
summary: CGP Grey argues for picking a theme for the year or season instead of setting goals or new year's resolutions. He explains how a theme gives direction without a pass/fail target.
why_hn: A staple recommendation in new year and goal-setting threads, with many commenters adopting yearly themes.

title: The essence of calculus
summary: The first video of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Calculus series, which builds toward integrals, derivatives, and the fundamental theorem of calculus from a simple geometry question. It aims to make viewers feel they could have invented calculus themselves.
why_hn: A staple recommendation for anyone learning math, praised for visual intuition that makes memorized formulas make sense.

title: Dick Proenneke in Alone in the Wilderness
summary: A condensed film of Dick Proenneke's footage of building a cabin and living alone in the Alaskan wilderness, using hand tools and local materials. It draws on the 8mm films he shot himself.
why_hn: HN recommends it often and warmly, as an inspiring and peaceful view of self-reliance and handcraft, in threads on cabins, solitude and woodworking.

title: Mike Monteiro: F*ck You, Pay Me
summary: Mike Monteiro's CreativeMornings talk on getting paid for creative and freelance work, covering contracts, working with lawyers, and refusing to work for free. It is delivered with blunt humor.
why_hn: HN regulars send freelancers and consultants to it whenever clients don't pay or contracts come up.

title: CppCon 2014: Mike Acton "Data-Oriented Design and C++"
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Mike Acton of Insomniac Games argues that a program's purpose is transforming data, and shows how common C++ approaches work against that in performance-critical game development. He covers cache behavior, data layout and the limits of compilers.
why_hn: It is the go-to talk HN points to for data-oriented design and hardware-aware performance thinking, despite Acton's blunt style.

title: RSA ANIMATE: Changing Education Paradigms
summary: An RSA Animate drawn from a Sir Ken Robinson talk arguing that current education systems are modeled on the industrial age. It discusses divergent thinking, standardization, and how schools disengage kids.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible, widely shared critique of schooling, and cites it in threads on ADHD, creativity and education reform.

title: Mindfulness with Jon Kabat-Zinn
summary: Jon Kabat-Zinn leads an hour-long Google tech talk on mindfulness, introducing the basic ideas and including a guided meditation. It is aimed at newcomers.
why_hn: For over a decade HN has pointed people asking about stress, focus or meditation to this as a restful and approachable introduction to mindfulness.

title: Is Most Published Research Wrong?
summary: Veritasium explains why a large share of published research findings may be false, covering p-values, p-hacking, publication bias and low replication rates. It draws on John Ioannidis's well-known paper and describes reforms such as preregistration.
why_hn: HN commenters link it whenever a shaky study or the p<0.05 threshold comes up, as a short primer on false positives in science.

title: 30 Essential Ideas you should know about ADHD, 1A Intro, Chronic Developmental Disability
summary: The first clip from Russell Barkley's 30 Essential Ideas about ADHD series, introducing ADHD as a chronic developmental disability. It is part of a lecture series on the disorder by a leading ADHD researcher.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly recommend Barkley's lectures as the best introduction to understanding ADHD.

title: Category Theory 1.1: Motivation and Philosophy
summary: The first lecture in Bartosz Milewski's category theory series for programmers. It covers the motivation and philosophy behind category theory and why composition matters for handling complexity.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly name it as the friendliest entry point to category theory for working programmers.

title: Richard Feynman Fire
summary: A short clip from a Richard Feynman interview in which he explains fire, describing how burning wood releases sunlight stored by the tree, which built itself mostly from air. It showcases his curiosity and plain-spoken explanations.
why_hn: HN repeatedly cites it as an elegant, eye-opening explanation of fire and photosynthesis and as an example of Feynman's infectious love of knowledge.

title: This is how you treat ADHD based off science, Dr Russell Barkley part of 2012 Burnett Lecture
summary: A short excerpt from Dr Russell Barkley's 2012 Burnett Lecture on ADHD, focused on treatment. He argues ADHD is a disorder of executive function and self-regulation, and that environments should be designed to compensate.
why_hn: HN people with ADHD or ADHD-affected relatives share it as an authoritative, practical talk that helped some seek diagnosis.

title: Václav Smil at Driva Climate Investment Meeting 2019
summary: Vaclav Smil's talk on historic energy transitions and what they imply for climate investment. He argues that transitions are slow, technology improves gradually, and only absolute cuts in energy use would truly work.
why_hn: Frequently linked as a sobering, data-grounded counterpoint to techno-optimism about decarbonization and green growth.

title: Stop Writing Classes
summary: Jack Diederich's PyCon 2012 talk argues that classes are overused in Python and walks through real code, refactoring away unnecessary classes, exceptions and modules. It popularized the heuristic that a class with two methods, one being __init__, should be a function.
why_hn: HN returns to it repeatedly as the canonical argument for simplicity and against premature abstraction, and several commenters say it changed how they write code.

title: Joe Rogan Experience #1109 - Matthew Walker
summary: Joe Rogan interviews Matthew Walker, Berkeley neuroscience professor and author of Why We Sleep. They discuss what sleep does for the brain and body, the effects of sleep deprivation, and sleep myths.
why_hn: HN readers recommend it as an accessible, motivating summary of Why We Sleep for people who will not read the book.

title: Your Brain Thinks Your Whole Home Is One Room
summary: CGP Grey argues that your brain treats a whole home as one room during lockdown, blurring work, rest and leisure. He recommends creating separate spaces and routines for different activities to stay balanced.
why_hn: HN recommends it constantly in work-from-home, burnout and procrastination threads as practical advice for separating work from life at home.

title: The man with 1,000 Klein Bottles UNDER his house - Numberphile
summary: Numberphile visits Cliff Stoll, the man behind ACME Klein Bottles, and sees how he stores a thousand glass Klein bottles in a crawlspace under his house. A remote-controlled forklift fetches them.
why_hn: HN commenters love Cliff Stoll's earnest, playful personality and point to this as a delightful look at his unusual warehouse.

title: Building a realistic artificial sun (for dark winter days)
summary: DIY Perks builds a realistic artificial sun for dark winters, using a powerful water-cooled LED, a satellite dish reflector for near-parallel rays, and a scattering layer to mimic the blue sky. The video explains the optics behind why most lamps do not look like sunlight and shows the build and its results.
why_hn: Whenever HN discusses seasonal affective disorder, myopia, or bright home lighting, people point to this as the most convincing buildable example of sunlight-like illumination.

title: Why Heat Pumps are Immensely Important Right Now
summary: Technology Connections explains why heat pumps matter right now, covering their efficiency, how they hold up in cold weather and the energy savings over burning fuel. It follows his earlier explainer on how they work.
why_hn: HN's default link for anyone asking whether heat pumps work and why they're efficient, thanks to the presenter's clear and enthusiastic delivery.

title: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford Commencement Address
summary: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford commencement address, told through three stories: connecting the dots, love and loss, and death. It includes the calligraphy class and the 'stay hungry, stay foolish' close.
why_hn: HN returns to it for motivation and perspective, and quotes it constantly, especially the connect-the-dots and remembering-death passages.

title: May 1, 1969: Fred Rogers testifies before the Senate Subcommittee on Communications
summary: Seven-minute footage of Fred Rogers testifying before a US Senate subcommittee in 1969 to defend federal funding for the new Corporation for Public Broadcasting. A skeptical Senator Pastore starts out abrasive and is won over during Rogers' brief, calm testimony.
why_hn: HN commenters hold it up as a model of persuasive public speaking and as the go-to reminder of why public broadcasting deserves funding.

title: Tiedustelueverstin arvio Venäjästä | 3.12.2018
summary: A 2018 lecture, with subtitles available, by former Finnish intelligence colonel Martti J. Kari on Russian strategic culture. He walks through the historical layers of Russia and explains why the country behaves as it does.
why_hn: After the 2022 invasion, commenters spread it widely as an eye-opening explanation of Russian mindset, corruption and propaganda, though a few doubt the presenter's rigor.

title: Essence of linear algebra preview
summary: A five-minute preview of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, which uses animation to build geometric intuition for topics from a standard linear algebra course.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends the series as the best intuition-first, visual introduction to linear algebra and a benchmark for clear math explanation.

title: Analogy as the Core of Cognition
summary: Douglas Hofstadter's Stanford Presidential Lecture argues that analogy is the core of cognition, illustrating how concepts, categorization and thought arise from analogy-making.
why_hn: HN regulars treat it as an essential, fun Hofstadter talk for any discussion of concepts, analogy and metaphor.

title: How to green the world's deserts and reverse climate change | Allan Savory
summary: Allan Savory's TED talk arguing that desertification of grasslands can be reversed with holistic managed grazing, which he says would also help reverse climate change. TED notes that other scientists have challenged his claims.
why_hn: HN commenters bring it up in climate and food threads as a hopeful, if contested, idea about grazing and soil carbon.

title: 34C3 -  The Ultimate Apollo Guidance Computer Talk
summary: Michael Steil and Christian Hessmann's 34C3 talk explaining the Apollo Guidance Computer end to end: hardware design, operating system, and mission software.
why_hn: Repeatedly called the best and most comprehensive AGC talk, with commenters rewatching it and treating it as foundational computer architecture learning.

title: Can YOU Fix Climate Change?
summary: Kurzgesagt examines what individuals can do about climate change, covering lesser-known carbon sources and why systemic and political change matter more than personal footprints.
why_hn: Cited in climate threads to argue that individual action is not enough and that political pressure is needed.

title: Powers of Ten™ (1977)
summary: The Eames Office's 1977 film Powers of Ten starts at a picnic in Chicago and zooms out by a factor of ten every ten seconds to the edge of the universe. It then zooms inward to a proton in a carbon atom.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as the classic visualization for building intuition about scale, and it comes up whenever a thread concerns scale or size comparisons.

title: Sunlight: Optimize Health and Immunity (Light Therapy and Melatonin)
summary: Dr. Roger Seheult of MedCram reviews the benefits of sunlight beyond vitamin D, covering the solar spectrum, circadian rhythm, melatonin and infrared light. The lecture runs nearly two hours with timestamps.
why_hn: HN cites it as an accessible physician-led review supporting claims about infrared light, mitochondria and morning sun.

title: A Swift Introduction to Geometric Algebra
summary: An animated introduction to geometric algebra, presented as a language that can describe most of physics. It was made with manim and covers multivectors and how they generalize familiar tools like cross products and quaternions.
why_hn: HN calls it the best video on geometric algebra, one that makes the subject click in about 40 minutes.

title: The hardest problem on the hardest test
summary: 3Blue1Brown walks through a very hard Putnam competition problem and its elegant solution, emphasizing the visual intuition and the thought process behind solving it.
why_hn: HN fans list it among their favorite 3Blue1Brown videos for showing how mathematical problem solving actually unfolds.

title: Imaginary Numbers Are Real [Part 1: Introduction]
summary: The first part of Welch Labs' series on imaginary numbers, presenting them as the natural extension of the number line into two dimensions. It covers the history and the math with strong visuals.
why_hn: HN commenters rate the series as some of the best visual teaching on complex numbers and recommend it for building intuition.

title: TempleOS | Down the Rabbit Hole
summary: Fredrik Knudsen's 86-minute documentary on Terry A. Davis, creator of TempleOS, tracing his work, his schizophrenia and his decline. It is a chronological video essay built on his public posts and videos.
why_hn: Regarded as the definitive, if heartbreaking, account of Terry Davis and TempleOS.

title: Seattle is Dying | A KOMO News Documentary
summary: A one-hour 2019 KOMO News documentary hosted by Eric Johnson on Seattle's homelessness and drug crisis, with interviews and looks at proposed solutions including a drug court program in Rhode Island. It argues addiction and mental illness are at the core of the problem.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it in homelessness threads about San Francisco and Seattle as an eye-opening, widely viewed argument for treatment-first policy, though some see it as pro-law-enforcement framing.

title: Life in Syntropy
summary: A short film from Agenda Gotsch introducing syntropic agriculture and Ernst Gotsch's agroforestry methods, made for COP21. It shows degraded land regenerated into productive forest farms.
why_hn: HN users repeatedly offer it as the best introduction to agroforestry as a climate and food solution.

title: The Egg - A Short Story
summary: Kurzgesagt animates Andy Weir's short story The Egg, in which a person learns that they are every human who has ever lived. It adds music and narration to the original text.
why_hn: HN commenters call it a beloved story and link the animation when threads touch on consciousness, empathy or identity.

title: Once you understand game theory, you understand the world.
summary: Veritasium explores the Prisoner's Dilemma and Axelrod's tournaments, showing why tit-for-tat and forgiving strategies win in repeated games. It extends the ideas to cooperation in evolution and conflict.
why_hn: HN commenters reach for it constantly as an approachable explanation of why cooperation and reciprocity are rational strategies.

title: Master Your Sleep & Be More Alert When Awake
summary: Andrew Huberman's podcast episode on what makes us sleepy, helps us sleep soundly and keeps us alert. It lays out the science and a set of behavioral tools such as light timing.
why_hn: HN users repeatedly credit it with fixing their sleep, especially its advice on morning light and dimming lights in the evening.

title: Eating less Meat won't save the Planet. Here's Why
summary: Joseph Everett, with Dr. Frank Mitloehner, argues that eating less meat will not do much for the climate. He covers beef's water footprint, land and feed use, and methane.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a counterpoint to claims about beef's environmental cost, though some critique its methane argument.

title: Frank Abagnale | Catch Me If You Can | Talks at Google
summary: Frank Abagnale, the real subject of Catch Me If You Can, speaks at Google about his life as a con man turned FBI fraud and cybersecurity expert, including advice on fraud, breaches and credit cards.
why_hn: Praised as a charismatic, engaging talk with practical security lessons, like why credit cards protect you better than debit cards.

title: Brown; color is weird
summary: Technology Connections explains why brown is not a spectral color but a context-dependent perception, essentially dark orange seen against brighter surroundings.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as a surprisingly magical explainer on color perception, often cited in color-space discussions.

title: NaN Gates and Flip FLOPS
summary: Tom Murphy (suckerpinch) presents a deliberately trollish computer architecture built on IEEE-754 floating point, using NaN and infinity to define logic gates. He builds working hardware around the idea.
why_hn: HN fans hold it up as a favorite among his videos and an example of gloriously bonkers technical art, and cite it in floating-point discussions.

title: This is Financial Advice
summary: Dan Olson's long Folding Ideas video on the GameStop meme stock phenomenon, its online community and the conspiracy thinking around it. It runs over two hours.
why_hn: Recommended as a thorough, sober critique of meme-stock culture and a good starting point whenever GameStop news appears.

title: Why Are You So Angry? Part 1: A Short History of Anita Sarkeesian
summary: The first part of Innuendo Studios' six-part video essay series on the online hostility around Anita Sarkeesian and GamerGate. It lays out the history and the motivations of the people involved.
why_hn: HN recommends the series as a nuanced analysis of online harassment, defensiveness, and gaming culture conflict.

title: #HITB2012KUL D1T3 - The Grugq - OPSEC: Because Jail is for wuftpd
channel: Hack In The Box Security Conference
summary: The Grugq's Hack In The Box 2012 talk on operational security for hackers, drawing on hacker indictments and counter-intelligence research. It reviews OPSEC goals and methods for avoiding detection and arrest, with case studies of how hackers got caught.
why_hn: HN treats it as the go-to talk on OPSEC and pseudonymity, recommended in threads about Tor, Silk Road and staying anonymous online.

title: Lecture: 2017 Maps of Meaning 01: Context and Background
summary: The first lecture of Jordan Peterson's 2017 Maps of Meaning course, setting out the Cold War context for his theory of belief and culture. He introduces the narrative structure of culture and archetypal characters for the individual, the known and the unknown.
why_hn: Several HN commenters credit the lecture series with helping them through depression or personal collapse and recommend it as long-form learning.

title: The 7 Habits of Highly Miserable People
summary: CGP Grey's sarcastic animated video adapted from the book How to Be Miserable, listing habits that reliably make people unhappy. By inverting the advice, it shows what to avoid and prompts reflection on goals and routines.
why_hn: HN recommends it widely in advice threads on depression, habits, and goal setting as a funny, memorable way to see what to do by seeing what not to do.

title: Michael Moore Presents: Planet of the Humans | A Film by Jeff Gibbs | Full Documentary
summary: Planet of the Humans, a full documentary by Jeff Gibbs presented by Michael Moore, arguing that the green movement has been co-opted by corporate and wealthy interests and that techno-fixes are not enough.
why_hn: HN uses it as a contrarian critique of renewables and green tech, often recommended with caveats about bias and flawed conclusions.

title: DOUGLAS ADAMS: Parrots, the Universe and Everything
primary_topic: douglas adams on nature and extinction
summary: Douglas Adams gives a talk at UCSB, recorded shortly before his death, about the odd lives of animals and what they suggest about humanity's future. It draws on his Last Chance to See work and is funny and wide-ranging.
why_hn: Adams fans repeatedly call it one of his best talks, a funny and moving look at extinction and the environment.

title: Incels | ContraPoints
summary: ContraPoints' 35-minute video essay on incels, examining the community, its worldview and how people get radicalized. It is delivered with theatrical style and an empathetic tone.
why_hn: Recommended as an empathetic, non-judgmental analysis of incel radicalization and how to counter it.

title: Everything is a Remix (Original Series)
summary: Kirby Ferguson's video essay series arguing that creativity is built on copying, transforming and combining existing work. It covers music, film and technology, then turns to copyright and patents.
why_hn: HN invokes it constantly in debates over originality, copyright and AI training, and calls it the best explanation of creativity as remixing.

title: The Art of Code - Dylan Beattie
summary: Dylan Beattie's NDC London talk on code written for art, fun and curiosity rather than utility. It includes quines, live music programming with Sonic Pi, and a memorable closing.
why_hn: HN regularly names it among the best programming talks ever, praising the storytelling, the demos and the ending.

title: Why It Was Almost Impossible to Make the Blue LED
summary: Veritasium tells the story of how Shuji Nakamura and others made the blue LED, long thought nearly impossible. It covers the materials challenge of gallium nitride and the persistence it took.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a gripping story of single-minded persistence against the herd, and as the back story behind modern LED lighting.

title: Richard Feynman Computer Science Lecture - Hardware, Software and Heuristics
summary: A lecture by Richard Feynman on how computers work, using the analogy of a filing clerk that becomes progressively dumber and faster. It also covers heuristics and how computers handle data and solve problems in finite time.
why_hn: Frequently recommended as the clearest plain-language explanation of what a computer fundamentally is, with at least one commenter saying it changed how they think about programming.

title: The determinant | Chapter 6, Essence of linear algebra
summary: A 10-minute 3Blue1Brown chapter explaining the determinant as the factor by which a linear transformation scales area or volume. It builds the idea geometrically with animations before any formulas.
why_hn: HN repeatedly points people to it as the clearest visual intuition for determinants, often saying it finally made the concept click.

title: I Genetically Engineered *MYSELF* to Fix Lactose Intolerance
summary: The Thought Emporium's host describes making and taking a DIY gene therapy to treat his own lactose intolerance. It uses an AAV virus to deliver DNA coding for the lactose-digesting enzyme, made with biohacker Gabriel Licina's help.
why_hn: HN keeps citing it as the standard example of accessible DIY gene engineering and self-experimentation, in threads on gene therapy, CRISPR and biohacking.

title: What your Differential Pairs Wish You Knew with Rick Hartley - AltiumLive Keynote
summary: Rick Hartley's AltiumLive keynote on differential pairs in PC boards. He argues the rules from cables and twisted pairs do not carry over, and covers which pair geometry gives the best impedance control, the right spacing, routing practice and how much skew is acceptable.
why_hn: HN engineers cite Hartley as the intuitive, field-based alternative to cargo-cult PCB advice, especially on differential pair routing, reference planes and EMI.

title: Ira Glass on Storytelling 3
summary: A five-minute clip of Ira Glass on the gap between good taste and early creative work. He says beginners know their work falls short and must keep producing to close the gap.
why_hn: HN commenters return to it as motivation for creators who feel their work is not good enough yet.

title: The EU Has Orbits, and the UK Fell Out of All of Them
summary: CGP Grey's six-minute explainer of the relationships the UK could have with the EU, based on Barnier's slide, shown as orbits of different closeness. It explains why the UK's red lines ruled out the closer options.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the quickest clear overview of the Brexit options, though later commenters note it predates the final outcome.

title: It’s Time To Break Up With Our Gas Stoves | Climate Town
summary: Climate Town argues for moving away from gas stoves. It covers the gas industry's decades of marketing and lobbying, health effects of gas cooking, methane leaks, and the case for induction.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it in gas stove and induction threads for exposing how the idea that gas is better for cooking was a marketing ploy.

title: The Machinery Of Freedom: Illustrated summary
summary: An illustrated 23-minute summary of David Friedman's talk based on The Machinery of Freedom. It describes how law, police and courts could work as market services in a stateless society, covering private law, polycentric law and objections.
why_hn: HN commenters use it as a short introduction to anarcho-capitalist ideas about private law and how disputes could be resolved without a state.

title: NVC Marshall Rosenberg - San Francisco Workshop - FULL ENGLISH SUBTITLES TRANSCRIPTION
summary: A roughly three-hour San Francisco workshop by Marshall Rosenberg on Nonviolent Communication, with full English subtitles added by a fan. He teaches the model with his jackal and giraffe language examples.
why_hn: HN commenters send people to it as the primary source for NVC, recommended for relationships, compassion and difficult conversations.

title: The Psychology of Human Misjudgement - Charlie Munger Full Speech
summary: Audio of Charlie Munger's 1995 Harvard speech on the psychology of human misjudgment, laying out a framework of cognitive biases and mental models for decision making. It covers factors like incentives, social proof and denial.
why_hn: HN regards it as a classic to revisit every few years for improving decisions and self-awareness.

title: Brainwash: The Gender Equality Paradox
summary: An episode of the Norwegian documentary series Brainwash, in which a comedian interviews academics from different sides about gender differences and gender equality. It looks at why more equal societies can still show unequal career choices.
why_hn: Recommended in HN threads on gender gaps in tech as a well-researched look at how gender differences and professional choices may arise.

title: Guided Wim Hof Method Breathing
summary: An 11-minute guided Wim Hof breathing session built around an expanding and contracting bubble to pace the breath. Wim breathes along with the viewer over ambient sound.
why_hn: HN commenters share it as an easy-to-follow guided exercise for anxiety, stress, and recovery, with many reporting daily use.

title: MountainWest RubyConf 2013 Devs and Depression by Greg  Baugues
summary: Greg Baugues tells his story of living with bipolar II and ADHD as a developer at a Ruby conference. He urges openness about mental illness and explains how to get help and support colleagues.
why_hn: Repeatedly recommended in mental health threads for its honest storytelling that resonates with developers.

title: Unix and Google
summary: A short animated simulation comparing how Multics and Unix were developed, showing why Unix's small composable programs and pipes gave it a efficiency advantage. It frames Unix as a moonshot achievable by a small team.
why_hn: Cited constantly in threads on microservices, composability and the Unix philosophy as a compact explanation of why small interoperable pieces win.

title: Ep. 1 - Awakening from the Meaning Crisis - Introduction
summary: The first episode of John Vervaeke's lecture series on the modern meaning crisis, tracing its history through philosophy, cognitive science, religion and psychology. It introduces the series and its themes.
why_hn: HN recommends the series as a thorough, non-dogmatic look at meaning, spirituality and escaping nihilism.

title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (in plain English)
summary: Okta developer advocate Nate Barbettini explains OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect in a roughly hour-long talk. It starts from the problems the protocols solve and walks through the flows. The description notes the implicit flow material is now out of date.
why_hn: HN repeatedly points people to it as the clearest way to finally understand OAuth, to the point that one team made it required viewing for new hires.

title: What Alcohol Does to Your Body, Brain & Health
summary: A two-hour Huberman Lab podcast episode on the physiological effects of alcohol on the brain and body at different levels of consumption. It covers genetic predisposition to alcoholism, alcohol metabolism, and how it causes cellular stress and changes thinking and behavior.
why_hn: HN commenters say it convinced them to quit or cut down on drinking, and point to it as a more comprehensive treatment than most articles.

title: The LED Traffic Light and the Danger of "But Sometimes!"
primary_topic: led traffic lights and technology criticism
summary: Technology Connections explains how LED traffic lights, which do not melt snow, drew complaints and were blamed for accidents. He uses it to illustrate the 'but sometimes' fallacy against new technology.
why_hn: Cited constantly as the name and example of the 'but sometimes' argument, where edge cases are used to resist better technology such as EVs and solar.

title: Gwynne Dyer -- Geopolitics in a Hotter World
summary: Historian and journalist Gwynne Dyer gives a long UBC talk on how climate change will reshape international politics. He covers food, borders, refugees and the possibility of unilateral geoengineering by affected nations.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a sobering, still-relevant look at the geopolitical consequences of warming, including why official reports lag the data.

title: LEADERSHIP LAB: Writing Beyond the Academy 1.23.15
summary: Larry McEnerney of the University of Chicago Writing Program argues that good writing is defined by what readers value, not by rules or the writer's own ideas. He explains why academic habits fail outside academia and how to write so readers find the work valuable.
why_hn: HN treats it as the definitive writing lecture and recommends it repeatedly, with several commenters saying it changed how they write.

title: James Powell: So you want to be a Python expert? | PyData Seattle 2017
summary: James Powell's nearly two-hour PyData talk builds up Python's data model, decorators, generators and context managers, coding live in Vim. It aims to take intermediate programmers toward real Python expertise.
why_hn: HN calls it one of the best technical talks and the clearest explanation of decorators, generators and context managers.

title: Manufactured Discontent and Fortnite
summary: Dan Olson of Folding Ideas critiques Fortnite's monetization, arguing it uses manufactured discontent, such as shop design and skins, to push spending. The video dissects the psychological techniques behind the game's business model.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as the definitive critique of Fortnite's monetization and of manipulative free-to-play design.

title: The Voting System That's Actually Too Good for Politicians to Allow
summary: CGP Grey explains the Single Transferable Vote, a proportional ranked-ballot system, and why politicians have little incentive to adopt it. It is a short animated explainer of how multi-winner ranked voting works.
why_hn: HN's default link for explaining STV in any thread on voting reform, ranked choice or gerrymandering.

title: Darius Kazemi, Tiny Subversions - XOXO Festival (2014)
summary: Darius Kazemi's XOXO 2014 talk on releasing 72 weird internet side projects in a year. Framed as 'How I Won the Lottery,' it argues that success needs both luck and buying many tickets.
why_hn: HN uses it as the favorite antidote to survivorship-bias success stories, arguing that trying many cheap things raises your odds.

title: Toward Rational, Authentic Food Choices | Melanie Joy | TEDxMünchen
summary: Psychologist Melanie Joy's TEDxMunchen talk introduces carnism, the invisible belief system that conditions people to eat some animals but not others, and how it shapes reactions to food choices.
why_hn: Recommended in vegetarian and animal-welfare threads as an introduction to the psychology behind how we treat animals differently.

title: Erlang The Movie II: The Sequel
summary: A humorous 10-minute parody sequel to Erlang: The Movie, in which Erlang's creators discuss the aging language and meet a surprise helper. It plays on the Outlaw Techno Psychobitch joke for OTP.
why_hn: HN loves it as a funny, shorter sequel and even uses it to introduce Erlang in university classes.

title: On The Turing Completeness of PowerPoint (SIGBOVIK)
summary: A short SIGBOVIK 2017 presentation by Tom Wildenhain showing that PowerPoint animations are Turing complete, with a working Turing machine built in slides. The talk is delivered deadpan as a serious research result.
why_hn: HN repeatedly names it as one of the funniest and best talks, a favorite example of absurd computation.

title: You Actually Share Your Brain With a Silent Stranger
summary: CGP Grey explains split-brain patients, where severing the corpus callosum lets the two hemispheres act independently. He uses this to explore the idea of two minds in one head.
why_hn: HN returns to it constantly in consciousness and decision-making threads as a clear, entertaining explanation of split-brain.

title: Carl Sagan - Pale Blue Dot
summary: Carl Sagan's narration of the Pale Blue Dot passage, reflecting on the Voyager photograph of Earth as a tiny speck in space. It is a short meditation on humanity's smallness and shared home.
why_hn: HN commenters return to it for perspective, comfort and Sagan's soothing voice, and suggest watching it periodically.

title: Chicken chicken chicken
summary: Doug Zongker's deadpan conference presentation of his famously chicken-filled paper, given at the 2007 AAAS humor session. It satirizes academic talks while showing the pitfalls of bad presentation.
why_hn: Beloved as a humor masterpiece and often cited as required viewing on what not to do in an academic talk.

title: Thinking outside the 10-dimensional box
summary: 3Blue1Brown visualizes high-dimensional spheres to explain a surprising puzzle about how a sphere fits in a box as dimensions grow. It builds geometric intuition for counterintuitive properties of high-dimensional space.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the go-to intuitive visualization of high-dimensional geometry, relevant to machine learning, optimization and sphere packing.

title: The Physics and Philosophy of Time - with Carlo Rovelli
summary: Physicist Carlo Rovelli gives a public lecture at the Royal Institution on how our understanding of time has changed, from Boltzmann and Einstein to quantum theory and loop quantum gravity. He blends physics, philosophy and art to argue that time is stranger than everyday intuition suggests.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a lucid, general-audience lecture that shows how wrong common conceptions of time are, often in threads on entropy and the arrow of time.

title: Millennials Don't Exist! Adam Conover at Deep Shift
summary: Adam Conover's talk at a millennial marketing conference argues that generations are an unscientific, condescending idea and that millennials do not exist as a real category. The description notes that researcher Jean Twenge later said he misrepresented some of her work.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it when arguing that generational labels are marketing inventions used to belittle groups.

title: Veritasium: What Everyone Gets Wrong About AI and Learning – Derek Muller Explains
summary: Veritasium's Derek Muller gives a Perimeter Institute livestream on how AI might change teaching and learning. He draws on past technology shifts and cognitive science to argue that learning requires effortful repetition.
why_hn: Recommended as a balanced take on AI and education, with the point that learning takes work that no technology can do for you.

title: Debate Noam Chomsky & Michel Foucault - On human nature [Subtitled]
summary: The full 1971 Dutch television debate between Noam Chomsky and Michel Foucault on human nature, with subtitles. They discuss creativity, knowledge, power and politics.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a famous, revealing clash between two thinkers, though some note they largely talk past each other.

title: Dani DaOrtiz at Fool US 2022 (the act that Penn and Teller didn’t even try to figure out.)
summary: A ten-minute card-magic act by Dani DaOrtiz performed on Penn & Teller: Fool Us in 2022. It is built on timing, misdirection and psychology, and the method defeated the show's hosts.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly call it among the best magic performances ever, valuing it as acting and craft that stays impressive even once you know the method.

title: I don't like notebooks.- Joel Grus (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
summary: Joel Grus's JupyterCon talk explaining why he dislikes Jupyter notebooks. He covers hidden state, trouble with reproducibility and testing, and how notebooks frustrate teaching. He shows his preferred workflow and what Jupyter could change.
why_hn: It is the go-to funny, irreverent critique of notebooks, linked whenever HN debates notebooks versus testable code.

title: Optimistic Nihilism
summary: Kurzgesagt's short animated take on optimistic nihilism. It argues the universe has no inherent meaning, so we are free to create our own and enjoy life.
why_hn: HN users recommend it as a comforting, clear introduction to nihilism for anxiety, mid-life doubts and feeling behind in life.

title: Joscha Bach: Artificial Consciousness and the Nature of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #101
summary: Lex Fridman has a three-hour conversation with Joscha Bach about artificial consciousness, the workings of the mind, intelligence and the possibly simulated nature of reality.
why_hn: Praised as a long but rewarding conversation, with commenters especially liking Bach's emphasis on modelling as a skill and his bridge between mind and computation.

title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | Chapter 14, Essence of linear algebra
summary: 3Blue1Brown's chapter on eigenvectors and eigenvalues in the Essence of Linear Algebra series. It builds a visual intuition for what they mean, why an eigenbasis is useful, and ends with a puzzle.
why_hn: HN repeatedly names it the best, most intuitive explanation of eigenvalues, and a gateway to the whole linear algebra series.

title: Jonathan Blow: Video Games and the Human Condition
summary: Jonathan Blow's 2010 Rice University talk argues that game designers refine their techniques in ways that can manipulate players, as with A/B-tested social games. He discusses the ethical responsibility of designers and what games can offer beyond addiction.
why_hn: Recommended as a thoughtful critique of addictive game design and the designer's role in building ethical games.

title: Why Is It So Hard to Do Something That Should Be Easy? (Wall of Awful pt. 1)
summary: A short How to ADHD explainer, featuring Brendan Mahan, on why simple tasks can feel impossible for people with ADHD. It introduces the 'wall of awful', a pile of past failures, shame and anxiety that builds up in front of a task and blocks starting it.
why_hn: HN commenters use it as the go-to name and explanation for task paralysis and procrastination, and say it helped them see why they avoid tasks.

title: Intelligence and Stupidity: The Orthogonality Thesis
summary: Robert Miles explains the orthogonality thesis: how an agent can be highly intelligent while pursuing goals that seem stupid or alien to humans. He separates intelligence from goals and touches on the stamp-collector example.
why_hn: HN people use it as the standard short explanation for why AI can understand human ethics without sharing them, and often recommend the whole channel.

title: The best stats you've ever seen | Hans Rosling
summary: Hans Rosling uses the Gapminder animated-data tool to debunk myths about world development, with sportscaster-like energy. It shows trends in health, income and child survival across countries.
why_hn: HN invokes it as the classic evidence that the world has improved and that people misjudge it, and as an example of great data presentation.

title: How to Invent the Future I - Stanford CS183F: Startup School
summary: Alan Kay's Stanford Startup School lecture covers his career at Xerox PARC and how to think about inventing the future. He goes through what came out of PARC and why companies fail to capitalize on such ideas.
why_hn: It is HN's standard answer to questions on creativity, finding problems and PARC history, valued for Kay's thinking about thinking.

title: Dr. Robert Zubrin with a brilliant answer to "Why Should We Go To Mars?"
summary: A short clip of Dr. Robert Zubrin, author of The Case for Mars, answering why humanity should go to Mars. He argues that societies grow by challenging themselves and that exploration inspires young people.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly link it as the best concise answer to the question of why go to Mars when problems remain on Earth.

title: Steve Jobs Secrets of Life
summary: A short excerpt from a 1994 interview of Steve Jobs in which he says everything around us was made up by people no smarter than you, and that you can change and shape the world.
why_hn: Quoted in threads on motivation, agency and regret as an encouraging reminder that the world can be changed.

title: Why We Won't Raise Our Kids in Suburbia
summary: Not Just Bikes argues that car-dependent suburbs rob children of independence, contrasting North American suburbia with Dutch cities where kids walk and bike on their own. It is the creator's remake of an earlier video on the topic.
why_hn: The standard link in threads about child autonomy, helicopter parenting and car-centric planning.

title: "The Hard Parts of Open Source" by Evan Czaplicki
summary: Evan Czaplicki, creator of Elm, discusses the hard parts of running an open source project: online community conflict, why its patterns arise, and a cultural history of open source. He offers ideas for more civil, productive communication.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an insightful look at the people side of open source maintenance, especially in Elm and maintainer-burnout threads.

title: 7 Habits For Effective Text Editing 2.0
summary: Vim creator Bram Moolenaar's 2007 Google Tech Talk on habits for efficient text editing. He explains how to spot repetition and inefficiency, then use editor features to fix it.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a lasting philosophy for improving your editing process incrementally, and it was widely remembered after Moolenaar's death.

title: CppCon 2017: Titus Winters “C++ as a "Live at Head" Language”
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Titus Winters' CppCon 2017 talk argues for C++ and Google's Abseil to be maintained as a live at head language, relying on testing and automated tooling rather than never changing or promising no compatibility. It covers Hyrum's law and the limits of semantic versioning.
why_hn: Recommended whenever versioning, semver, monorepos and backward compatibility are debated, for its nuanced treatment of dependencies.

title: James Burke Connections, Ep. 4 "Faith in Numbers"
summary: Episode 4 of James Burke's Connections series, tracing how commercialism, climate change and the Black Death shaped the move to the Renaissance. It follows threads through waterpower, the printing press, the Jacquard loom and the Hollerith punch card toward modern computing.
why_hn: HN commenters strongly recommend it for its account of how the Jacquard loom and punch cards led to computers.

title: Google I/O 2009 - The Myth of the Genius Programmer
summary: Brian Fitzpatrick and Ben Collins-Sussman argue that the 'genius programmer' ideal harms collaboration. They advocate trading ego for growth, sharing work early, and understanding how tools shape social behavior.
why_hn: HN regulars recommend it as a career-shaping talk on code review, humility and collaborative development.

title: The Great Global Warming Swindle Full Movie
summary: A 2007 Channel 4 documentary by Martin Durkin arguing that human-caused global warming is overstated or a scam. It features contrarian scientists such as Richard Lindzen and promotes sunspot and cosmic-ray explanations for temperature change. Its claims are rejected by mainstream climate science.
why_hn: Climate-skeptic commenters link it as evidence against the CO2 consensus, while others cite it as an example of climate-change denial.

title: The Expert Myth
summary: Veritasium examines which experts have real expertise, drawing on chess research and work by Klein and Kahneman. It explains that expertise comes from pattern recognition built through deliberate practice in valid, feedback-rich environments.
why_hn: Frequently recommended in threads on learning, the 10,000 hours rule and deliberate practice as a clearer account of how expertise develops.

title: How to sound smart in your TEDx Talk | Will Stephen | TEDxNewYork
summary: Will Stephen's humorous six-minute TEDx talk shows presentation techniques that make you sound brilliant while saying essentially nothing.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a funny deconstruction of TED talk style, and as a favorite example of the appearance of meaning without content.

title: The Battle of Midway 1942: Told from the Japanese Perspective (1/3)
summary: Part one of Montemayor's animated-map documentary on the Battle of Midway, told using only the information available to the Japanese side. It focuses on Nagumo's dilemma.
why_hn: HN recommends it for its information-dense maps and voice-over and for showing how commanders decide with limited information.

title: A CONSERVATIVE solution to global warming (Part 1)
summary: Potholer54 presents the climate science case and a market-oriented, conservative-friendly approach to addressing global warming, with sources listed. It is part one of a two-part series.
why_hn: HN users recommend it as a model of communicating climate science to conservative and libertarian audiences without alienating them.

title: "Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers: Stress and Health" by Dr. Robert Sapolsky
summary: Robert Sapolsky's lecture on how the body's stress response, evolved for short-term physical emergencies, harms long-term health when triggered by psychological stressors. It was given as the inaugural Fenton-Rhodes Lecture.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an entertaining and informative explanation of how stress affects health.

title: Brains, Sex, and Machine Learning
summary: Geoffrey Hinton's Google Tech Talk linking machine learning to biology, explaining dropout as a form of model averaging and why sexual reproduction and stochastic spiking neurons may prevent overfitting.
why_hn: Recommended as a simple, elegant explanation of dropout and its connection to how the brain works.

title: Dr. Gabor Maté — Trauma, Addiction, Ayahuasca, and More
summary: A long Tim Ferriss podcast interview with physician Gabor Mate on trauma, addiction, depression, ADHD and ayahuasca. Mate explains how childhood stress and emotional pain underlie many addictions and illnesses.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a thoughtful, honest look at the causes of addiction and depression, and as a deeper Mate interview than most.

title: Copying Is Not Theft - Official Version
summary: Nina Paley's one-minute animated free culture anthem with vocals by Connie Champagne, arguing that copying is not theft.
why_hn: Linked constantly in copyright and piracy debates as a short explainer of the difference between copying and physical theft.

title: Orbital Rings
summary: Isaac Arthur explains the orbital ring, a megastructure launch-assist system that could move bulk cargo cheaply to orbit and beyond. He compares it with space elevators and discusses power transmission.
why_hn: HN commenters offer it as the likely future of cheap access to space, feasible without exotic materials.

title: 38C3 - From Silicon to Sovereignty: How Advanced Chips are Redefining Global Dominance
summary: A 38C3 talk on how advanced chips are made, centered on EUV lithography and the global supply chain behind it. It covers technical challenges from raw materials to finished chips and the geopolitical weight of semiconductors.
why_hn: HN users recommend it as an excellent, accessible overview of how modern chips are produced and why EUV matters.

title: golden balls. the weirdest split or steal ever!
summary: A Golden Balls episode in which one contestant announces he will steal, leading to an unexpected outcome in the split-or-steal prisoner's dilemma.
why_hn: The canonical real-world example in game theory discussions of manipulating a prisoner's dilemma.

title: In Search of Tomorrow
summary: Chris Granger, creator of Light Table and the Eve language, gives a Berkeley data science lecture on what computation and programming might look like in ten years. He covers the path that led to Eve and ends with demos.
why_hn: HN keeps pointing to it as a thoughtful vision of programming for non-programmers and as background on Eve's motivations.

title: Bret Victor - The Humane Representation of Thought
summary: Bret Victor's closing keynote at UIST and SPLASH 2014 argues that our tools for thinking ignore most of human sensory and motor capability. He sketches representations that engage more modalities beyond screens and keyboards.
why_hn: HN treats it as a foundational Bret Victor talk that reshaped how people think about software and interfaces, often cited alongside Dynamicland.

title: Timothy Snyder: The Making of Modern Ukraine. Class 1: Ukrainian Questions Posed by Russian Invasion
summary: The first class of Timothy Snyder's Yale course on the making of modern Ukraine. It introduces the course and asks what it means for a nation to exist in light of the Russian invasion.
why_hn: Strongly recommended as an accessible, well-taught history of Ukraine and a counter to propaganda narratives.

title: Visualizing the 4d numbers Quaternions
summary: 3Blue1Brown builds visual intuition for quaternions, showing how to think about this four-dimensional number system using stereographic projection and rotations in 3D space. It is part one of a two-part series with an interactive companion site.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as the best visual explanation of quaternions and a good way to visualize higher dimensions.

title: How Valve is Profiting from Steam's Back-Door Casinos
summary: People Make Games investigates the unregulated CS:GO skin gambling economy and Valve's role in it. It includes interviews with people who lost large sums and examines why Valve does not intervene.
why_hn: HN recommends it as well-researched reporting on skin gambling, especially its effect on minors, in threads about gambling and Valve.

title: DjangoCon 2008 Keynote: Cal Henderson
summary: Cal Henderson's DjangoCon 2008 keynote, "Why I Hate Django", is a funny critique of Django from a Flickr architect. It touches on scaling topics such as database replication.
why_hn: Recommended as a brilliant, hilarious talk, though not the most educational.

title: We're building a dystopia just to make people click on ads | Zeynep Tufekci
summary: Technosociologist Zeynep Tufekci argues that the machine-learning systems used to serve ads also decide what political and social information people see. She explains how opaque algorithms can nudge, segment and manipulate users, and warns that the real danger is powerful people using AI to control populations.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it whenever engagement-optimizing feeds, micro-targeting or ad infrastructure come up, as an accessible warning about algorithmic amplification.

title: These Stupid Trucks are Literally Killing Us
summary: Not Just Bikes explains how SUVs and light trucks have grown in size and share of US sales, and why that is dangerous for pedestrians, cyclists and city life. He covers the regulatory loopholes, such as fuel economy rules and the chicken tax, that favored them.
why_hn: It is HN's default link whenever vehicle size comes up, with commenters recommending it for the history of the light-truck loophole and the safety effects of tall bumpers.

title: Visualization of Quantum Physics (Quantum Mechanics)
summary: An animated visualization of basic quantum mechanics using a free particle, with simulations based on the actual equations. It covers waves, particles, and how measurement collapses the wavefunction.
why_hn: HN commenters call it one of the best visual explanations of the wave, particle and measurement relationship, free of silly metaphors.

title: Can You Watch This Without Getting Angry?
summary: CGP Grey explains how ideas spread like germs, and why content that triggers outrage spreads fastest, using a study on what makes online content viral. He argues that opposing outrage-driven memes feed each other.
why_hn: HN links it constantly in threads on social media, polarization and outrage as the canonical explanation of why angry content wins.

title: The Biggest Myth In Education
summary: Veritasium debunks the idea of learning styles, such as being a visual learner, with an interview with Daniel Willingham and a memory experiment. It argues that a multimodal approach helps everyone.
why_hn: The standard link whenever someone claims to be a visual learner or learning styles come up, with sources listed in the description.

title: Alex Evans at Umbra Ignite 2015: Learning From Failure
summary: Media Molecule's Alex Evans recounts the journey, including the failures, of finding the Dreams engine, based on his Siggraph 2015 talk. It covers the signed-distance-field and splat-based rendering approach and the artistic goals behind it.
why_hn: HN calls it an inspirational must-see on SDF rendering and a favorite tech talk for graphics programmers.

title: Jancovici : Can we save energy, jobs and growth at the same time ? 08/01/2018
summary: Jean-Marc Jancovici lectures at ENS Paris on whether energy use, jobs and growth can all be preserved. He argues for a physical approach to economics, since resource depletion and climate limits make perpetual GDP growth unrealistic.
why_hn: Recommended as a sober, physics-based account of how energy underlies the economy.

title: How to Invent the Future II - Stanford CS183F: Startup School
summary: Part two of Alan Kay's Stanford Startup School lecture on inventing the future. He draws on his time at Xerox PARC and elsewhere to discuss how to think about new technology and what makes ideas useful.
why_hn: Frequently suggested in Ask HN threads on finding ideas, creativity and why incumbents like Xerox missed what they invented.

title: The first 20 hours -- how to learn anything | Josh Kaufman | TEDxCSU
