summary: Josh Kaufman's TEDx talk argues that you can reach practical competence in almost any skill with about 20 hours of focused practice, rather than the 10,000 hours often quoted. He describes how becoming a parent led him to rethink how adults learn, and lays out a short method for rapid skill acquisition.
why_hn: HN uses it as the standard counterpoint to the 10,000-hour rule and as an encouraging recipe for starting new skills.

title: The Lottery: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
summary: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment on state lotteries. It argues that the claim that lotteries fund education is misleading, because the money is fungible and often diverted to general funds.
why_hn: Go-to reference in lottery threads for the point that earmarked lottery revenue does not really add to school funding.

title: Stanford Lecture: Don Knuth—"A Conjecture That Had To Be True" (2017)
summary: Donald Knuth's 2017 Christmas Tree Lecture at Stanford about a combinatorial geometry problem whose computed numbers matched a striking formula. He tells the story of the conjecture and its sequel.
why_hn: HN fans love it for Knuth's humor and for how he makes open math problems feel approachable, and it is often cited for details like dancing links and counting rectangle subdivisions.

title: "Two incompatible sacred values in American universities" Jon Haidt, Hayek Lecture Series
channel: Duke University Department of Political Science
summary: Jonathan Haidt's Hayek Lecture at Duke argues American universities pursue two potentially incompatible sacred values, truth and social justice. He discusses campus conflict, honor, dignity and victimhood cultures, and viewpoint diversity.
why_hn: HN cites it heavily in diversity and academia debates as an intellectual analysis of the truth versus social justice conflict.

title: You Suck at Excel - Joel Spolsky (Reupload)
summary: A reupload of Joel Spolsky's talk teaching spreadsheet users the Excel features they are probably missing, such as keyboard navigation, named ranges, tables and lookups. The original disappeared and this copy comes from the Wayback Machine.
why_hn: HN commenters call it an internet classic that makes you a more proficient Excel user, and note it is still relevant despite predating newer functions like XLOOKUP.

title: We WILL Fix Climate Change!
summary: Kurzgesagt's animated take on climate change argues that, despite alarming headlines, there are real reasons for hope as technology, policy and public attitudes shift. It surveys trends and solutions while acknowledging the scale of the problem.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an articulate, uplifting counterweight to climate doomerism, though one critic calls it a form of denialism and another notes it omits nuclear.

title: P vs. NP and the Computational Complexity Zoo
summary: An 11-minute animated introduction to P vs. NP and the wider landscape of complexity classes, inspired by the Complexity Zoo wiki. It assumes no background in computer science.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the best short, funny introduction to P vs. NP and complexity classes for people with no background.

title: K Lars Lohn - Keynote - PyCon 2016
summary: K Lars Lohn's PyCon 2016 keynote weaves together music theory, programming, biking road trips and fractals. It is a personal, wide-ranging talk rather than a Python how-to.
why_hn: Commenters call it a mind-blowing, beautiful talk and cite it among their favorite tech talks.

title: Zebras All the Way Down - Bryan Cantrill, Uptime 2017
summary: Bryan Cantrill's Uptime 2017 talk on the engineering challenges of the stateful data path, including storage, firmware and hardware bugs. It uses the 'zebras vs. horses' diagnostic heuristic to explain why rare failures keep appearing.
why_hn: A perennial HN favorite whenever firmware, disks, ECC or opaque hardware come up, valued as both entertaining and sobering.

title: Simulating an epidemic
summary: 3Blue1Brown builds toy SIR models to simulate how an epidemic spreads and tests scenarios like social distancing, travel restrictions, central gathering places and quarantine. It was made during the early COVID-19 outbreak.
why_hn: HN pointed to it during 2020 as a digestible, well-made illustration of epidemic dynamics and interventions.

title: The Secret History of Silicon Valley
summary: Steve Blank tells how World War II, Stanford's Frederick Terman and military and intelligence agencies shaped the rise of Silicon Valley. The talk centers on the Cold War electronic warfare and signals intelligence work that seeded the region's tech industry.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an eye-opening, once-secret history of where Silicon Valley came from, and cites it whenever the military roots of tech come up.

title: Traffic Has a Perfect Solution. Humans Are the Problem.
summary: CGP Grey explains how traffic jams come from human driving behavior such as tailgating and reaction delays, and how leaving gaps and smoothing speed would reduce congestion. It also touches on self-driving cars.
why_hn: HN cites it as a concise, well-illustrated explanation of traffic flow, in threads on congestion, self-driving cars and driving habits.

title: England: South Sea Bubble - The Sharp Mind of John Blunt - Extra History - Part 1
summary: The first part of Extra History's animated miniseries on the South Sea Bubble. It explains how England's government debt led Robert Harley to turn to financier John Blunt, whose schemes began inflating artificial demand for shares.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible, easily digestible introduction to the South Sea Bubble whenever financial manias, ICOs or overvalued companies come up.

title: Propaganda Games: Sesame Credit - The True Danger of Gamification - Extra Credits
summary: An Extra Credits episode on China's Sesame Credit, which gamifies obedient citizenship through a social score. It covers how the system rewards conformity and pressures people through their friends' behavior.
why_hn: HN commenters use it as a short, accessible primer on social credit and surveillance-driven gamification, linking it in many privacy and China threads.

title: The Collapse of The American Dream Explained in Animation
summary: A 30-minute animated film explaining how money, banking and the Federal Reserve work and arguing that the American economy is heading for collapse. It is opinionated and has a strong point of view.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible animated primer on banking and the Fed, usually with the caveat that it is biased and dated.

title: ElixirConf 2018 - Docker and OTP Friends or Foes - Daniel Azuma
summary: Daniel Azuma's ElixirConf 2018 talk on whether Docker and OTP conflict. He shows they can coexist and uses Horde and DeltaCrdt, with a live tank-game demo, to keep state alive across container kills.
why_hn: Recommended for its practical strategy for preserving state on ephemeral containers, and for the live demo.

title: James Baldwin Debates William F. Buckley (1965)
summary: The 1965 Cambridge Union debate between James Baldwin and William F. Buckley Jr. on whether the American Dream comes at the expense of the American Negro. It is a historic recording of the two speaking.
why_hn: Recommended for Baldwin's riveting delivery and as an example of serious debate between opposing worldviews.

title: Emacs Org-mode - a system for note-taking and project planning
summary: A 2008 Google Tech Talk by the creator of Org-mode, introducing the Emacs subsystem for plain-text note-taking and project planning. It covers outlines, TODO states, tags, dates and priorities, and later shows using Org-mode as a spreadsheet.
why_hn: HN regards it as the best introduction and advertisement for Org-mode, and many say it was enough to get them started with it.

title: Randy Pausch Lecture: Time Management
summary: Carnegie Mellon professor Randy Pausch gives a lecture on time management at the University of Virginia in 2007. He covers practical habits such as tackling important tasks first and distinguishing important from urgent work.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a practical, memorable guide to prioritization, and some rewatch it every year.

title: GigCityElixir23 - Bryan Hunter
summary: Bryan Hunter's GigCityElixir 2023 talk on HCA Healthcare's Waterpark system, built on Elixir/Erlang. It describes how the architecture is distributed and fault-tolerant, with a multi-datacenter cluster and runtime code swapping.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a rare real-world look at a large fault-tolerant Erlang/Elixir system with no downtime in healthcare.

title: Patrick Stewart interview - Parkinson - BBC
summary: Patrick Stewart on the BBC's Parkinson talk show talks humorously about going bald, how it affected his career and relationships, and how he came to accept it.
why_hn: HN recommends it in hair-loss threads as a funny, inspiring example of accepting baldness.

title: Alexander Pope Wrote a 35-Page Takedown of a Historian
summary: CGP Grey tells the story of Alexander Pope's long takedown of a historian, Thomas Hearne, framed around the quirks of library books and archival research. It is a funny, digressive video essay about literary feuds and tracking down original sources.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a masterpiece of humorous archival detective work and a great watch about books and libraries.

title: The Caretaker - Everywhere At The End Of Time - Stages 1-6 (Complete)
summary: The complete six-stage album series Everywhere at the End of Time by The Caretaker, about 6.5 hours of music that depicts the progression of dementia through distorted, decaying old ballroom recordings.
why_hn: HN recommends it, often emotionally, as an auditory depiction of memory loss, in threads about dementia and aging.

title: Why Electric Bikes are More Dangerous than Motorcycles
summary: FortNine argues that e-bikes have injury rates and speeds closer to motorcycles than to pedal bikes. It argues riders should treat them with similar safety gear and caution.
why_hn: Cited repeatedly in e-bike threads as a well-argued safety counterpoint from someone who rides both.

title: Evo-Devo (Despacito Biology Parody) | A Capella Science
summary: A Capella Science parody of Despacito that sings through evolutionary developmental biology, explaining how a single cell becomes a body, including body-axis genes and dormant snake leg DNA. It runs about four minutes.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an entertaining four-minute introduction to evo-devo that works even for people who dislike the original song.

title: Feeding Bill Gates a Fake Burger (to save the world)
summary: Mark Rober makes a plant-based burger for Bill Gates and explains why meat production strains the environment. Gates also appears and discusses his worry about steel and cement.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a short, accessible overview of the climate and water case for plant-based meat.

title: Pure Functional Programming in Excel • Felienne Hermans • GOTO 2016
summary: Felienne Hermans argues that Excel is the world's most popular programming language and shows how spreadsheets work as a pure functional language. She implements a few mathematical problems in spreadsheet formulas to illustrate why they are so powerful and approachable.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it whenever Excel, spreadsheets or functional programming come up, as a fun and serious take on spreadsheets as real programming.

title: Heat Pumps are Not Hard: Here's what it will take to start pumping
summary: Technology Connections' long closing video in his heat pump series, arguing that adopting heat pumps is well within reach. It explains how they work and what it takes to start using them.
why_hn: HN recommends the series as an enthusiastic, entertaining deep dive into residential heat pumps whenever heating or climate threads arise.

title: Opioids: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
summary: A Last Week Tonight segment on the US opioid epidemic, tracing how prescription painkillers fed addiction and heroin use. It is the first of three episodes the show devoted to the crisis.
why_hn: HN points to it as an informative, fact-heavy overview of the opioid crisis and Purdue Pharma.

title: Do Nothing- a message of motivation from Self-help Singh- (un) motivational speaker and life coach
summary: A short satirical 'motivational' talk by the character Self-help Singh, a sham life coach who urges viewers to do nothing. It parodies self-help gurus and hustle culture.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as funny anti-motivational comedy that also touches on real truths about productivity and the rat race.

title: The Web That Never Was - Dylan Beattie
summary: Dylan Beattie's entertaining NDC talk imagines an alternate history of the web, asking what if different decisions had been made on operating systems, browsers and standards. It blends real history with humor.
why_hn: HN commenters strongly recommend it as a fun alt-history of the web and bring it up whenever people muse about how the web could have been different.

title: How lucky is too lucky?: The Minecraft Speedrunning Dream Controversy Explained
summary: Matt Parker analyzes the Minecraft speedrunning controversy in which Dream was accused of cheating via improbably lucky drops. He walks through the probability and the statistical arguments in the original accusation and the reply.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an engaging lesson in probability and in how statistics can expose cheating.

title: Admiral Grace Hopper Explains the Nanosecond
primary_topic: latency and the speed of light
summary: Admiral Grace Hopper holds up a length of wire to show how far light travels in a nanosecond, about 11.8 inches. She explains how she made the idea concrete to people who could not picture a billionth of a second.
why_hn: HN uses it to illustrate physical latency limits and why performance and distance matter in computing.

title: The Carbon Offset Problem
summary: Wendover Productions examines why carbon offsets so often fail to reduce emissions, covering specific examples and the perverse incentives in offset schemes.
why_hn: Recommended in greenwashing and offset threads as a well-sourced, detailed explanation of how offsets underdeliver.

title: [JSConfUS 2013] Steven Wittens: Making WebGL Dance
summary: Steven Wittens' JSConf US 2013 talk on drawing with WebGL, using animated visuals to walk through vectors, matrices and the rendering pipeline. Despite the title, it works as a visual primer on the linear algebra behind 3D graphics.
why_hn: HN treats it as one of the best intros to the math of 3D graphics and a staple answer to how to learn graphics programming.

title: Uppestcase and Lowestcase Letters  [advances in derp learning]
summary: Tom Scott-style absurdist research by tom7 for SIGBOVIK 2021, using machine learning to discover letterforms that are 'uppercaser' than uppercase A and lowercaser than lowercase. It is a comedic, technically inventive deep dive with fonts and a paper.
why_hn: Tom7 is an HN favorite, and this video is praised as hilarious, educational silly ML that keeps getting better.
